key_claim: The Vogt–Russell theorem says mass and composition set a star's structure, which holds as a good approximation for most stars but not universally.

slides.headline: A star's whole structure, set by two things
Mass and ingredients decide the rest
slides.body: The Vogt–Russell idea says a steady star is shaped by two things: its total mass and what it is made of. That includes its radius and luminosity.

slides.headline: The idea sat unpublished for years
slides.body: Vogt had the idea in 1926 but published in 1931. Russell, working alone, published the same idea in 1931.

slides.headline: Then the models found exceptions
slides.body: Later studies found that near some limits, or with instabilities, the same mass and mix can give many solutions. So the idea is not universal.

slides.headline: Even a “theorem” can be a first guess.
slides.body: For most ordinary stars, mass and makeup give one stable answer.

caption:
A star's whole structure, set by two things

Two things, a star's total mass and what it is made of, are said to set its whole structure when it is in steady balance. That is the Vogt–Russell idea. Heinrich Vogt formed it in 1926, but his first paper came in 1931. Russell developed it on his own.

The catch? Later studies found that near some limits, or with instabilities, the same mass and mix can give many solutions. So the idea is not universal.

The payoff? For most stars under normal conditions, like main-sequence stars, the models settle on one stable answer. That is why it still works as a first approximation. 🌟
